correctness.rationale: With r=n−k+1 overlapping linear reads, the t-th offset count is the source sum over [t,t+r−1], so neighboring offset counts differ by w_(t+r)−w_t. Each residue chain with any nonzero difference is fixed by that difference and propagation in both directions. For k>k*, integer rounding gives n≥4r−1, so at most one chain has length three and every other chain has length ≥4 (for r=1 the sole chain has n≥8 sites). A constant chain of at least four sites cannot contain ones, and the remaining weight determines the only possible constant length-three chain. At the claimed boundary, n=hr+b, h=2 or 3, 0≤b<r. In the h=2 branch there are b≥2 valid weight-three phases: n≥4r−5 gives b≥2r−5 for r≥4, and n≥8 gives b≥2 for r=3. For h=3 there are r−b≥2 valid phases since n≤4r−2. A phase change permutes the r read-start residues, so the entire ordered-within-read multiset agrees even though the linear words differ. This proves the last ambiguity, not all smaller lengths. An independent direct enumeration of the 56 weight-three words at n=8 found ambiguities at k=1,2,3,4,6 and injectivity at k=5,7,8, supporting the remark about nonmonotonicity. The two frozen verification ranges are only checks of the proof, not its basis; the uploaded code was read, not run.

value.rationale: Three markers are a natural fixed-sparsity test for reconstructing a linear word from its contiguous reads. The exact last ambiguous length is useful because smaller read lengths need not behave monotonically. The offset-marginal result is a substantive reduction in required data, and the periodic full-deck witnesses show that the upper guarantee cannot be improved even when the complete ordered contents of all reads are available.
